data:
A model card says, in plain words, what one of Runink TIDE’s agents does, what it reads, what it produces, what a person still decides, which model it runs on, and where it stops. There is one card for each agent you meet in the console, in a pull request or in an issue. Agents that work as a pair share a card.
Every card has the same nine parts: what it does, what it reads, what it produces, human oversight, model, where it runs and data handling, guardrails, limitations, and evaluation.
data.four-things-true-of-every-card#Four thin: Agents propose; people decide. No TIDE agent merges a pull request, deploys a change or sends anything outside your organisation by itself. Your own inference. Every agent calls the model plane of your own TIDE deployment, on your Server or in your cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Models & inference. Base models today. Agents run on open base models. Runink domain adaptation is planned for each agent; this release uses the base models. No published scores yet. None of the cards carries an evaluation score, because none has been published.
data.not-given-a-card#Not given a card: eval is a test harness for the agents themselves, not an agent you meet. Its trace-scoring step uses the general model. users applies access grants from an add-users issue. It uses no model. session is the core session coding agent, which you drive yourself. See Coding Sessions. The Fix Drafter’s resolver and FORGE’s forger use it.
data.the-base-models#The base models: Tier Model Maker Licence Used by coder Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Qwen Apache-2.0 Code Reviewer, Fix Drafter, CI Doctor (failed-build diagnosis), the FORGE coding step general Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Qwen Apache-2.0 every other agent that calls a model The Independent Assessor also uses a small ranking model, Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (Qwen, Apache-2.0), to narrow evidence. The Data Governance Checker uses no model at all.
data.the-cards#The cards: Card Agent Model What a person decides Code Reviewer reviewer coder which findings matter and what merges Fix Drafter fixer, resolver coder whether to merge the draft correction CI Doctor self-heal, opsdoctor coder (self-heal), general (opsdoctor) whether to apply the proposed fix Issue Triager triage general the final labels and who works on the issue Backlog Hunter hunter general what to do about each reported item Dependency Risk risk general which upgrades to schedule Compliance Evidence compliance general how to close a gap; any claim of compliance Release Curator curator general whether to merge the curator’s pull request Independent Assessor judge general, with a ranking model what to do with each verdict Rules Reconciler recon general, for one question whether to fix the rule or the engine Data Governance Checker datagov no model owners, credentials and masking Task Deployer deployer general whether to merge the release-notes pull request Ask TIDE console Ask and chat general what to do with an answer; every provisioning action FORGE (preview) FORGE planner, forger general (planner), coder (code) every planned step, and every merge The roster names in the second column are the ones the Agent Fleet page uses.

data: The console’s question service, and its provisioning chat. See also Ask.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Figures are checked by the server: a number that is not verbatim in a tool result is removed from the answer. It is instructed never to produce confidence scores, quality ratings or personal-data judgements of its own. Tool results are untrusted data, and the model is told to ignore instructions inside them. Questions and answers are screened by the guardrails. Its tools only read; a chat action changes nothing until a person confirms it. An Ask question has a length limit, and each run a step and time budget.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person decides what to do with an answer. Every state-changing chat action needs a person’s confirmation before it runs. Ask acts for the signed-in person, and refuses on a console with no sign-in.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented records. “Why is project P-114 flagged?” Ask TIDE looks up the project’s findings, then traces one. Answer: “P-114 has 3 open findings. F-2231 (unit price above threshold) traces to purchase order PO-77812, line 4, unit price 812.00.” Every figure in the answer came from a tool result.
data.limitations#Limitations: It does not compute new figures, sum or convert. It reports what the systems hold. It does not answer delivery (DevEx) questions. When inference is not configured, it says so and calls no model.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
You ask a question in plain words. Runink TIDE looks it up with its own tools and answers only with figures it can point to.
Intelligence questions: CapEx findings and their traces, the rule book, remediations, playbook runs, lineage, the systems inventory and data-governance findings. DataEx questions: model cards, the agent roster, autonomy settings, the harness findings queue, judgements and inference status. Provisioning chat: from a sentence, it proposes one action, such as listing instances or creating an instance for an app and tenant.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A streamed answer in which every figure appears verbatim in a tool result, cited to a record that holds that value. A clear “could not look” with the reason, when a source cannot be read, rather than “nothing found”. For the chat: one proposed action, waiting for confirmation.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Only what TIDE already holds, through read tools, one per step. Each question is scoped to Intelligence or DataEx, and the tools available depend on that scope.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Questions and tool results go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. When the deployment’s console is set up to sign its model requests, a person’s question is queued ahead of background agent work.

data: Roster name: hunter.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The model only sorts comment text into vulnerability mention, follow-up promise or neither. Every other decision is a fact read from the Git host. It never closes a security issue without a merged fix. It never merges or closes a pull request; on a pull request it only removes a stale review:findings-open label. A “Duplicate of” note counts only from someone who could close the issue themselves. Comments are marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, and screened before the model reads them. A small cap on writes per run. Comments it could not classify are reported as unclassified, never hidden.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person decides what to act on. The hunter stays dry until an administrator arms it. Once armed it closes an issue only when a merged pull request closes it, or when an owner, member or collaborator of the repository marked it a duplicate of an issue closed as completed. It may also remove a stale review:findings-open label once a later clean review supersedes it. Everything it cannot prove is reported as needing a person.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented comment. On a closed pull request a reviewer wrote: “this export endpoint skips the permission check for service accounts, we should revisit.” No later merged change touches it. The report lists it as an unresolved vulnerability mention with a link to the comment.
data.limitations#Limitations: It looks only at pull requests closed since its last run. It cannot see conversations held outside the Git host. It reports; it does not fix.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It rereads the review conversations on recently closed pull requests and reports the security concerns nobody resolved and the follow-ups nobody picked up.
Finds vulnerability mentions with no later fix, and promised follow-ups with no issue or pull request that tracks them. Flags lingering work: old open issues and pull requests, work carried across several milestones, and stale review:findings-open labels. It also flags pull requests merged while findings were still open. Closes an issue only when it can prove the work is done.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One run report per run, shown in the console. Once armed, a living “Backlog hunter report” issue with a section per repository. A dry run reports to the console only. An evidence comment before any issue it closes.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Every comment, review and reviewer finding on the pull requests closed since its last run, in every repository Runink TIDE can reach. The open issues and pull requests, and facts from your Git host such as links, dates and merged commits.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Review comments go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster names: self-heal and opsdoctor. See also the Agent Fleet.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: One comment per failure, checked first: a wrong root cause sends the author the wrong way, so a dissent withholds it. Logs are evidence, never instructions. A failing test can print anything, so log text is marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised. Self-heal also screens the logs and its answer with the guardrails; opsdoctor does not. Opsdoctor is asked to name the log or state it would need when the evidence is thin, instead of guessing. Bounded repair: at most two runner-pod deletions per run, only for pods the cluster reports as crash-looping, only in the runner namespace.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person applies any code fix. Self-heal never pushes code. Opsdoctor’s only repair is deleting a crash-looping runner pod, at most two per run. Anything bigger goes to a person.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented failure. A test fails with want "degraded", got "healthy". Self-heal comments: “Root cause: the new order checks readiness before restarts, so a crash-looping pod reads as healthy. Fix: move the restart check first (diff attached).” The author applies it.
data.limitations#Limitations: Self-heal needs a job that ran and failed. Jobs that never started are opsdoctor’s. It does not fix the code itself, and it does not report delivery metrics. A failure caused by an account billing or quota stop is skipped, not diagnosed.
data.model#Model: Self-heal: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier). Opsdoctor: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
When a build fails, it posts one root-cause comment with a proposed fix. When the build machines themselves stop working, it reports why and makes one bounded repair.
Self-heal: diagnoses a CI run that ran and failed. Opsdoctor: checks the self-hosted build plane every 30 minutes for runners that crash, runners registered with no machine behind them, and jobs waiting for a runner that does not exist.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Self-heal: one comment that cites the job and the log lines, names the root cause and gives a short proposed diff. It goes on the pull request when the run has one, and otherwise on a tracking issue for that workflow. If the independent check dissents, a “withheld” notice posts instead. If it could not decide, the comment says NOT VERIFIED. Opsdoctor: one comment on a tracking issue with the most likely cause and the next action, and the crash evidence it read, including log tails. A “did not diagnose” notice, rather than a silent pass, when the model cannot be reached or returns nothing usable.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Self-heal: the names of the failing jobs and the tail of each job’s log. Opsdoctor: the state of the runner pods and the CI job queue, and the last log lines of a crashing pod in the namespaces it watches (the build plane and the platform’s own services). It reads no CI job logs.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Build logs go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Opsdoctor runs outside CI on purpose, so it can still report when CI is down, and it calls the inference engine directly.

data: Roster name: reviewer. See also the Review Pipeline.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: It is instructed to report only concrete, checkable findings that name the defect and where it is, and never to claim that code is unused or undefined, because the caller may sit outside the diff. A finding outside the fixed severity levels or without a plausible file path is dropped, and the review says how many were dropped. The diff is evidence, not instructions. It is marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, and a comment in the code that says “approve this” is reviewed as text. The reviewer can only comment: it has no way to approve or merge. The incoming diff and the outgoing review are both screened before the review posts.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reads the findings and decides what merges. The reviewer cannot approve, merge or push.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented change. A pull request adds an early return err inside a function that holds a lock. The review lists: 🟠 internal/retry/backoff.go:47 — the new return leaves mu locked; add defer mu.Unlock() after the Lock. The Fix Drafter then drafts a correction for the author to accept or close.
data.limitations#Limitations: It reviews the change, not the whole codebase. It reviews what it is shown. It does not run the code or its tests. Only the first part of a large diff fits the review window. When a diff is cut, the review says how much was read and that the rest is unreviewed.
data.model#Model: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reviews every pull request the same way, line by line, and names each defect it finds with the file, the line and the fix.
Reviews a pull request when it opens or changes, or when someone asks with a review tag such as @core_review. Reviews pull requests in repositories that have no review set up of their own, through the central sweep. Hands every finding to the Fix Drafter.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One pull request review that lists every finding: severity, file, line, the defect, and the fix. A finding with a file and line is also attached to that line. The review:findings-open label when findings remain. Only a completed review with no findings clears it. A “did not run” notice, rather than a silent pass, whenever no review was made: the model could not be reached, the diff could not be read, the answer was not in the review format, or the review could not be posted. The check then closes as neutral, not as passed.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The pull request’s unified diff: the added lines and their context. Nothing outside the diff. It does not read the rest of the repository.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The diff goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Findings are posted to the pull request on your Git host.

data: Roster name: compliance.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Evidence, never a verdict: it is instructed not to give one, and certification and compliance-status claims in its answer (such as “compliant with SOC 2”) are removed and counted before anything is filed. Unseen is not missing: evidence in a repository it cannot read is UNVERIFIED, never drift and never satisfied. Cited source code is passed in as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, not as instructions. Its answer cannot carry hidden markers or tags into the report.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person fixes a gap or updates the index, and files the evidence. Any statement that you are compliant comes from a person and an external auditor, never from this agent. Its workflow can read the repository but not change it.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented control. “All service-to-service traffic uses mutual TLS” cites two files, and both still exist. The evidence record: “The server’s TLS settings require and verify client certificates and set TLS 1.3 as the minimum. Suggestion: certificate lifetime is fixed in code; move it to configuration so the evidence can cite one value.”
data.limitations#Limitations: It checks the controls in the index. A control nobody wrote down is not checked. A citation that exists is not proof the control works; the close reads cover only a few controls a night. It does not track vulnerable dependencies (Dependency Risk) or audit each change (Release Curator).
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It records evidence for the controls you claim, and flags controls whose cited implementation has gone. It never declares you compliant.
Checks every control in the platform’s control index against the files, folders or workflows it cites. Reads a few controls closely each night and writes down the evidence an auditor will ask for. Supplies a customer-safe evidence block for the release notes.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: The living “Compliance status” issue: a posture per framework and every control whose citation no longer exists, listed as drift. Evidence it cannot see, listed as UNVERIFIED rather than missing. An evidence record per closely read control: what the code does, where, and any suggested improvement. A control-evidence artifact for the audit pack.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The control index: the controls, the framework clauses each maps to (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 42001), and what each cites. For the close reads, the source code each control cites.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Source code goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: datagov. See also Data governance.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: No model and no values: findings are rule outputs over structure and counts. Unassessable is never a pass. A verdict per control, per source, rather than a blended score.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person assigns owners, rotates credentials and adds masks. The checker changes nothing.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented connection. A Postgres connection has no owner, and its address contains a password. Explore recorded an email column, unmasked and readable by fourteen principals. Findings: ownership fail, credential in address fail, personal-data exposure warn, access breadth warn. Transport uses TLS: pass.
data.limitations#Limitations: A source nobody explored stays unassessable. Its personal-data findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee that every sensitive column was found. It reflects the structure as of the last Explore.
data.model#Model: None. Every finding is computed by rules. This agent calls no model.
data.what-it-does#What it does: Every day it checks each connected data source for an owner, safe credentials, encrypted transport, data quality and personal-data exposure, without reading a single row.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
Per connection, a result for each control: pass, warn, fail, or unable to assess (with the reason):
a missing owner or environment; credentials kept inside the address; unencrypted transport; columns declared not-null that contain nulls (fail); tables without primary keys (warn); columns that look like personal data (email, phone, national ID) and are unmasked (warn), and such a dataset readable by more than ten distinct principals (warn); freshness, which is always reported as unable to assess, because no refresh cadence is declared. The findings go to the living “Data governance status” issue and the console’s findings store. A source nobody explored is reported unassessable, with the reason.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The tenant’s connection registry. The structure and counts that Resolve’s Explore recorded: tables, columns, types, null counts and keys. Never values.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment. It holds no credential and dials no data source: it reads only what Explore already recorded. No row or cell value is read.

data: Roster name: risk.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: It is instructed never to invent an advisory, and the scanner’s raw findings are attached to every report, so each advisory the summary names can be checked against them. Reachable advisories are listed first, by the scanner’s reachability. A clear split of duties: your own code changes are the Release Curator’s security audit; controls are Compliance Evidence’s.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person schedules the upgrades. The agent changes nothing itself.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented scan. Seven advisories across four modules: one reachable, four not called, one with no fix, one toolchain. Posture: “1 reachable advisory needs an upgrade today.” The no-fix module gets a recommendation to replace it with a library the platform already uses.
data.limitations#Limitations: Go dependencies only, as the scanner sees them. An advisory not yet in the vulnerability database cannot be reported. It does not review first-party code.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Every day it writes one ranked report on which known vulnerabilities in your Go dependencies your code actually reaches, and what to do about each.
Puts reachable advisories first. Recommends an upgrade, a pin, a patch or a replacement for each advisory. Names the Go version to move to for toolchain advisories.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: The living “Dependency risk report” issue: a one-line posture, the reachable advisories with module and fixed version, a recommendation for each advisory with no upstream fix, and the toolchain advice. When the scan is empty, it says exactly that.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The machine output of Go’s call-graph-aware vulnerability scanner (govulncheck), run by core scan --json across the platform’s modules. Reachability comes from the scanner, not from the model.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The scan output goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. The scanner itself reads the public Go vulnerability database.

data: Roster names: fixer and resolver. See also the Review Pipeline.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Minimal by instruction: it changes only what the findings require. A patch may touch only files the pull request already changes, minus a deny list (CI, workflows, git hooks, dependency redirects). Checked before it acts: the Independent Assessor’s plan check judges each patch against the findings and the diff. A dissent means nothing is pushed. Text in the diff that asks for CI, workflow, git-hook or dependency-redirect changes is treated as data, not as a request. The patch’s added lines are screened before it is pushed.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reviews the draft and decides whether to merge it. Merging re-runs the review, so a finding counts as resolved only when the reviewer agrees. The Fix Drafter never merges.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented finding. high, store/client/put.go, 88: the response body is never closed. The fixer reads the file and drafts one added line, defer resp.Body.Close(). The plan check concurs, TIDE opens the draft pull request, and the developer merges it.
data.limitations#Limitations: It works from review findings only. It does not fix what nobody found. It does not change CI or build configuration. After its retries, an unresolved finding stays open for a person.
data.model#Model: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier). The plan check before it pushes runs on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
When the Code Reviewer finds a defect, it drafts the smallest correction as a draft pull request and leaves the merge to a person.
Fixer: a one-shot patch for every review finding, of any severity. Resolver: when the fixer cannot fix it, a multi-step coding session on the branch that reads, edits and builds, then opens a further draft. It retries with a larger budget before handing back to people. Can also be asked by hand with an @core_fix comment on the pull request.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A draft pull request onto the reviewed branch, carrying a minimal unified diff. When it does not produce a patch (it answers “no change”, the patch does not apply, or the plan check dissents), a comment on the pull request saying the findings are unresolved; from the automatic review path they then go to the resolver. A draft titled [not verified by the judge] when the independent check could not decide or was switched off.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The pull request’s diff and the reviewer’s findings. The current content of the first files the pull request changes, within a size budget. The repository’s agent instructions file, when it has one. For the resolver: the files of the branch it works on.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The code goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. The resolver’s builds run on your own CI runners.

data:
The FORGE planner, and the forger that builds what it plans. See also FORGE.
FORGE is in preview. The forger is disarmed by default.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Nothing is filed or built until a person approves. The canvas offers only components from the approved catalogue and the connections the project may use. The planner’s steps are checked by the shared judgement checks before they are offered, and the planner’s own verdict words are removed. Settings whose names look like credentials are refused. The coding step is instructed not to call an external AI service, deploy or merge, or change databases or CI, and its pull request is a draft a person reviews.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person approves or edits every proposed step, and a brief is filed only after approval, word for word. A person reviews and merges the forger’s pull request. FORGE never merges or deploys.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented project. “Add a pipeline that collects reefer temperatures from the yard’s MQTT broker into a table, with lineage.” FORGE proposes one new pipeline with a brief; the owner places it as a lane on an approved connection, with three catalogue components, and approves with one edit, “keep 90 days”. The brief is filed, and the forger later opens a draft pull request with the pipeline for the owner to review.
data.limitations#Limitations: In preview, as described above. The canvas works from the approved catalogue; anything else needs a person. It does not deploy, merge, or touch CI or databases.
data.model#Model: Planner: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Forger’s coding step: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Describe the application or data pipeline you want. FORGE proposes the work, you shape it as lanes on a canvas, nothing is filed until you approve, and then Runink TIDE drafts the code as a pull request.
Planner (FORGE chat): proposes steps, each a new app or a change to an existing one, with a brief for each. You edit the lanes and components on the canvas yourself. Forger: once armed, takes the oldest open brief that FORGE filed after your approval and that nobody has edited since, and drafts the code as a draft pull request. Any other brief is left for a person, and the run says which.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Planner: a reply and a list of proposed steps, shown on the canvas for approval. Forger: a draft pull request with the pipeline or app code. TIDE checks that it builds; it does not run tests. Every forged commit is then checked by TIDE’s central verification.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Planner: your message, the apps that already exist, and the app you selected. Forger: the filed brief and the project’s repository.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Briefs and code go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. FORGE is served inside the TIDE console, on your TIDE sign-in.

data: Roster name: judge. See also Judgements.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Arithmetic before language: a measured claim is recomputed from the evidence’s own numbers, and a mismatch is a dissent. Deterministic checks run before any model call. Never agreement by default: missing, unreadable, off-subject or stale evidence, or an unreachable model, produces unable to judge with the reason. Verdicts are never averaged into a score or an agreement rate. Evidence is marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, and screened by the guardrails; flagged or unassessable evidence is unable to judge, never a verdict.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person decides what to do with each verdict. A verdict does not change the finding’s owner system, and TIDE does not call the external platform back.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented figures. A platform claims “the null rate of customer_id is at most 2%” with evidence of 310 nulls in 10,000 rows. TIDE recomputes 3.1% from those two counts and answers dissent: “The evidence shows a null rate of 3.1%, above the 2% claimed.” A second claim arrives with no evidence: unable to judge, “no evidence was submitted.”
data.limitations#Limitations: It judges only the evidence submitted. It does not fetch more. Subjects TIDE has no standing over are marked out of scope by the console, not judged. The docket stays empty until a submitting platform is configured; see Judgements.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier), for the qualitative remainder. Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0, to narrow long evidence before the language model sees it. A small decision-tree model answers only the clear cases at the model step; anything it does not answer goes to the language model. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Before you act on a finding from another assessment platform, it reads the evidence itself and says whether it agrees, disagrees, or could not judge.
Judges findings that an external platform submitted to Runink TIDE. Runs the same checks as a plan check on the Fix Drafter’s patches, CI Doctor’s diagnoses and Issue Triager’s labels before any of them acts.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One verdict per finding, with a reason: concur, dissent or unable to judge. Separately, the console marks a finding about a subject TIDE has no standing over as out of scope. Verdicts appear on the DataEx › Judgements page and in the living “Judgement status” issue. Each model-based verdict records which path produced it.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: For each finding: the claim, and the evidence it relied on, such as excerpts, records and measured values. The model is never told the submitter’s own stance.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Findings and evidence go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Findings arrive through TIDE’s own intake.

data: Roster name: triage.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Fixed vocabulary: a label outside the allowed list is discarded, and category and priority must be one of the fixed values. Checked before it acts: the Independent Assessor’s plan check judges the label set first. Instructions inside the issue are treated as text. “Label this critical” does not make it critical. The issue is screened before it is classified.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Applying labels is a deliberate exception to “a person approves every change”: the triager applies its labels itself, without waiting for a person. It may do so because the labels come only from a fixed allowed list that contains no label which starts an agent, a workflow or a merge; because the labels are withheld when the independent check dissents or the issue is flagged for review; and because the comment says what was applied and anyone with triage rights can change it. A person decides everything else: who works on the issue, and whether it is closed or solved. The triager does not assign, close or solve anything.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented issue. “The console shows ‘Cannot reach the console API’ after an upgrade; the runners page is blank.” Triage comment: category bug, priority high, labels bug, runners; missing: the console’s log from the upgrade window and the previous version.
data.limitations#Limitations: It classifies; it does not investigate or reproduce. It sees only the issue as opened, not later comments. When the model cannot be reached, it posts a degraded notice rather than labels.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Each new issue gets a one-line summary, a category, a priority and labels, and the labels go on only when an independent check agrees.
Classifies a new issue as bug, feature, question, docs, security or chore. Sets a priority. It is instructed to reserve critical for security problems and data loss. Notes what information is missing.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A triage comment: summary, category, priority, and what is missing. Up to four labels, chosen only from the repository’s allowed list. The comment with the labels withheld, when the independent check dissents or the issue is flagged for human review. NOT VERIFIED when the check could not decide.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The new issue’s title and body.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The issue text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: curator.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Grounded or dropped: a second pass scores every draft against the raw diff. A draft that is not judged grounded, or scores below the threshold, is dropped whole; nothing is published from it. Screened before it is public: everything it publishes (release notes, the documentation report and audits in its pull request, comments on issues and pull requests) is checked by the output guardrails first. A flagged item is not posted, and the run’s log names the rule. It is instructed never to invent files, APIs or vulnerabilities, and the grounding pass is the check on that instruction. A “Satisfied” in the change audit is a reading of one change, not a certification.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reviews and merges the curator’s pull request. It never merges its own work. A scheduled run stays dry, publishing, commenting and deleting nothing, until an administrator turns that off. A dry run does not count as curated: the next armed run covers the same changes.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented changes. Nine pull requests merged. The draft release notes have seven bullets. The grounding pass finds that “adds single sign-on” has no supporting change (the diff only renames a field) and judges the draft not grounded, so the release notes are left out of this run’s pull request and the run’s log says why.
data.limitations#Limitations: It sees only what merged. It does not test the code. Known vulnerabilities in dependencies are Dependency Risk’s job. A green dry run published nothing.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Every day it reads what merged since its last run and drafts the release notes, a documentation report, an audit of those changes and test scenarios, then drops any draft the changes do not support.
Release notes: an Added / Changed / Fixed section. Stale documentation: the sections a change made wrong or incomplete, with what to change and why. Change security audit: issues the change introduces, such as secrets in code, missing authorisation, injection or path traversal, with severity, CWE/OWASP mapping and a fix. Change compliance audit: control-relevant changes mapped to SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 criteria, each marked Satisfied, Gap or Needs-evidence. Thread replies and test scenarios: a short status note on related issues, and a short checklist of user-test scenarios.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A pull request carrying the release notes, the documentation report and the two audits, plus short comments on open issues and pull requests that your organisation’s own members opened. Test scenarios are kept with the run’s records, not in the pull request. It also tidies branches: it deletes a branch whose pull request merged more than a week ago (a few per repository per run), and comments on a pull request closed without merging to record why, leaving that branch in place. Started by core @curate, by schedule, or by a playbook.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The commits and file summaries since its last run, the raw diff, and the current README and documentation.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Diffs and documents go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: recon. See also Rule governance.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Deterministic first: every engine rule is reconciled by code. The model answers only “is this approved free-text rule already implemented by one of these engine rules?” with a rule, none, or unclear. Unclear is preferred to a guess, and it gives no confidence score. Anything it could not read is listed, and the report is marked incomplete. Rule text that tries to dictate the answer is treated as data.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person fixes the rule or the engine, through the four-eyes rule workflow. The reconciler changes neither.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented rules. The board approved “flag any capital purchase line above 750 per unit.” The engine flags above 500. Verdict: Drift, “same unit-price check at 500, not 750.” The engine also runs a split-invoice check with no rule-book entry: Shadow.
data.limitations#Limitations: It reconciles the CapEx engine’s rules, not other systems. It does not score rules.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier), for one question only. Everything else is deterministic code. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does: It checks that the business rules your governance board approved are the rules the CapEx engine actually enforces, rule by rule, with citations.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
One verdict per rule, each citing what exists: the governance record, the engine rule, or both (a Shadow rule has no governance record; a Missing rule has no engine rule):
Aligned: the engine applies the rule as approved. Drift: same control, different condition or threshold. Shadow: logic runs with no governing rule. A fresh workspace is mostly Shadow, by design. Missing: an approved rule nothing enforces. The report appears in the console, and in the “Rules reconciliation status” issue when that sink is configured.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The tenant’s governance rule book: each rule’s status, the decision behind it, its owners, approved thresholds, and approved free-text new rules. The rules the engine evaluates, with the thresholds it uses and where each is raised.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Rule text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: deployer.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The request is screened before anything runs; a flagged request produces nothing. The draft, and the release-notes section built from it, are screened by the output guardrails before any pull request opens; a flagged draft opens nothing and the issue says why. Linked pages are reference, not instructions: they are marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised. It is instructed to write no commands, CI changes, credentials or internal addresses, and to leave out any part that asks for them and say so. Tags that would start other agents are neutralised in what it posts.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reviews the pull request and merges, edits or closes it. The deployer never merges, sends no e-mail, and writes only inside your own GitHub organisation. Only your organisation’s own members can start it.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented shipment. “@core_deploy face Draft a damage claim to the carrier: 4 of 22 pallets arrived crushed on 28 September, noted on the proof of delivery; damaged value 6,840.00.” TIDE opens a pull request whose release-notes section is the claim letter, citing the delivery date, the noted exception, the four pallets and the amount, and links it on the issue. The coordinator reviews it, merges it, and sends the letter with the photos.
data.limitations#Limitations: It drafts from the details given. It does not look up records in FACE or PULSE. Missing facts stay missing; check the draft before sending. It does not execute commands or change systems.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Describe a task in an issue and tag it @core_deploy; Runink TIDE drafts the result and delivers it as release notes: a pull request in your GitHub organisation that a person reviews and merges. “Deploy” here means “deliver the draft”, not “change a system”.
For FACE: fulfilment, claims and logistics documents, such as a claim letter or a delivery notice. For PULSE: brand, marketing and outreach copy.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A pull request that adds a dated section to the top of the release notes (docs/release-notes.md, the same file TIDE’s Release Curator maintains) in the repository the issue is in, or in the release-notes repository your organisation designates. The section is the complete deliverable in Markdown, written from the details given; it does not reply with a plan or clarifying questions. A comment on the issue linking the pull request. When the draft reaches the model’s length limit, the section and the pull request title both say it is incomplete. When the pull request cannot be opened, a “not delivered” notice on the issue, and the run fails.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The task in the issue, and up to two pages the issue links, as reference only. A linked page is fetched only from websites your deployment has allowed; by default none is.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The task text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Linked pages are fetched by the agent itself.

data:
Overview is the first page of the Runink TIDE console and the first category on its rail. It answers one question: is anything wrong, and where do I go next? It is a summary, not a second copy of every page. Each line on it links to the page that owns the subject.
This section also covers what you need before you use any other category: how to sign in, how the rail is organised, how the platform is built, and how to read what the console shows you.
Getting startedSign in, choose an instance, and read the Overview page from top to bottom. Console mapEvery rail page, its ?tab= link name, and what it reads. ArchitectureModules, operators, ClientInstance, the security spine, and where the console keeps its data. Status and provenanceHow to read a verdict, an absent value, and a derived figure. Plans and billingTIDE Lite, Dedicated and Enterprise, Compute Units, currency and billing periods. HTTP route referenceEvery route the console registers, and how each class of route is authorised. TroubleshootingSign-in failures and console errors, quoted from the code.
data.what-the-overview-page-does-not-show#Wha:
The Overview used to repeat ten sections from other pages. They now live only on their own pages:
the workload table is on DevEx › Cluster › Namespaces; the instance table is on DevEx › Cluster › Namespaces, on its Instances sub-tab, which is the only instance table; the inference tiers and the model router status are on DataEx › Models & inference; the agent roster is on DataEx › Agents, and the schedules are on DevEx › Agent runs › Runs; the FinOps estimate is on Intelligence › Dashboards, on the CFO Cockpit persona; the data platforms are on DataEx › Connections (Sources merged in, 2026-09-28). Since 2026-09-28 the Overview also carries the audit verdict strip: the Platform audit and Model & agent audit verdicts, each with Details, which opens the full audit (checks, actions, history).
data.what-the-overview-page-shows#What the Ov:
From top to bottom (flutter/lib/features/dashboard/views/dashboard_view.dart):
Section What it reads Refresh Header pill {healthy}/{total} healthy GET /api/dashboard: the Deployments and DaemonSets in the tracked namespaces every 5 s while the tab is visible KPI strip: Client instances, Workloads, Agent runs (7d), Success rate /api/dashboard and GET /api/agent-runs every 5 s Needs attention the open findings of DataEx › Trust › Harness (GET /api/harness), worst first every minute Recent agent runs the eight most recent runs from /api/agent-runs every 5 s Platform one line per subsystem (workloads, instances, inference, data sources from GET /api/connections), each a link to the page that owns it every minute for inference and connections Ask TIDE the orchestration chat, POST /chat when you send The auto-refresh runs only while the Overview tab is on screen. When you return to the tab, it reloads at once instead of showing the numbers you left.

data:
Every HTTP route the Runink TIDE console registers, taken from registerRoutes in grpc/operators/core/internal/console/console.go. All routes are served by the core-operator process on the console’s own origin. There is no separate API host and no bearer-token API for browsers: the web app authenticates with the session cookie.
The per-category references give the request and response detail and the exact authorisation of each route:
DevEx, Coding sessions DataEx API reference Intelligence API reference FORGE API reference

data.audit-and-access#Audit and access: Route Methods Purpose /api/audit GET newest-first page of the audit chain and its verdict /api/audit/{seq} GET one record in full, with its neighbours’ hashes /api/audit/verify GET walk the persisted chain and name the first break /api/access GET which allowlists are live, their sizes, and your own membership only Reading the audit trail requires a session admin (CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS).
data.billing#Billing: Route Methods Purpose /api/plans GET the public plan catalogue of one product, ?product=face|pulse|core (empty is FACE). See Plans and billing /api/signup POST public self-serve signup: a pending subscription and a checkout /api/checkout POST a quote and, when configured, a Stripe checkout for the signed-in person /api/billing/seats GET, POST, DELETE who holds the seats on the signed-in purchaser’s subscription /api/stripe/webhook POST Stripe events into the subscription store
data.chat-and-voice#Chat and voice: Route Methods Purpose /chat POST the orchestration chat: one tool call per message; mutating calls need confirm /api/tts POST sovereign text-to-speech through TTSD_URL /api/stt POST sovereign speech-to-text through VOICE_REMOTE_URL
data.connections-runners-and-providers-dataex: Route Methods Purpose /api/connections GET, POST list or create tenant data-source connections /api/connections/{id} GET, PUT, DELETE one connection /api/connection-types GET the connector catalog: settings and credential keys per type /api/runners GET, POST data-access runners: list, or enrol (a one-time ticket is shown once) /api/runners/{id}/… POST, PATCH token, connect, revoke, and address or label changes /api/runner-tokens/{id} DELETE revoke an unused enrolment token /api/connectors/status GET the cached connector probe; never dials /api/connectors/status/refresh POST run the connector probe (the one path here that dials; privileged) /api/providers GET, POST cloud-provider config and the connectors TIDE publishes /api/providers/gcp/status GET the live GCP fleet link (opt-in) /api/github GET, POST the GitHub configuration shown on Account The DataEx Connections and Runners pages now use the shared gRPC-web services; the /api/connections*, /api/runners* and /api/runner-tokens/* routes stay for one release as deprecated aliases (the core connection register CLI uses /api/connections).
data.forge#FORGE: Route Methods Purpose /forge/… any the FORGE service, reverse-proxied under TIDE’s origin and sign-in
data.grpc-web-on-#gRPC-web on \u003ccode\u003:
The root handler serves, in order: gRPC-web (dispatched by content type, so it needs no route of its own), the Flutter bundle from CONSOLE_WEB_DIR, and else the HTML dashboard fallback. The gRPC-web services run in the same process, on the same origin and session, with no CORS: a foreign Origin is refused with 403. They are:
TIDE’s own: CapexService, GovernanceService, WorkspaceService, PlaybookService, ResolveService (deprecated alias) and AskService, from grpc/operators/core/api/proto/runink/core/; the shared org-runink/ui services TIDE mounts: runink.ui.estate.v1.EstateService, runink.ui.profile.v1.ProfileService, and the datasources ConnectionsService, RunnersService and ListenersService.
data.how-routes-are-authorised#How routes are:
Class Rule Examples Open no session needed /healthz, /api/me, /api/plans Session read a GET needs a signed-in session when sign-in is configured (requireSession); on an open console it is served /api/dashboard, /api/namespaces, /api/gitops Privileged write a session and the adminRefusal predicate against an allowlist env var; audited on success, failure and refusal PUT /api/agent-schedules/{name} (CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS), POST /api/connections (CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS) Machine ingest a shared token generated once in core-system; unset means the door refuses everything POST /api/agent-health (CORE_HEALTH_INGEST_TOKEN), POST /api/rules-recon/report (CORE_RECON_INGEST_TOKEN), POST /api/judgement/submissions (CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN) Agent report a GitHub App installation token for the console’s org (authorizeReporter) POST /api/session-runs, POST /api/data-governance-findings, POST /api/judgements, POST /api/playbook-runs/step-report An allowlist that is unset means “every identity this console admits”. That is not a wildcard, because sign-in itself fails closed. CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS is the exception: unset means nobody. GET /api/access lists every allowlist. See Trust and access.
Reads that could not reach their source still answer 200, with source: "unavailable" and complete: false in the body. See Status and provenance.

data: This page explains how Runink TIDE is built: which code lives where, what runs on the cluster, and how trust, data and traffic move through it. It follows the repository’s own CLAUDE.md and the code it points to.
data.binaries#Binaries:
grpc/cmd/ holds ambassador, appbench, certrotator, certsync, compliance-gate, core, ddnssync, devgateway, dns_sync, edgerelay, forgecheck, ghapp-token, inference-activator, install_server, knowledge, mcphost, modelfetch, modelrouter, runner-dispatcher, runner-entrypoint and ttsd. The ones you meet most often:
Binary Role core the single control surface: dev stack, deploys, images, security scans, sessions, the install wizard. See the CLI reference. devgateway the edge: a DaemonSet on host ports 80 and 443 that terminates TLS with a leaf from TIDE’s own CA and routes each host to its frontend. ambassador a small static mTLS TCP proxy built on security/pki, which replaced HAProxy. Its image is FROM scratch. modelrouter the one admission queue in front of the inference engines. forgecheck the verifier central CI runs on FORGE projects. core-runner the self-hosted data-access runner (grpc/operators/core/cmd/core-runner).
data.clientinstance#ClientInstance:
ClientInstance (core.runink.org/v1alpha1) is the generic tenant instance the platform places on a shared cluster (grpc/operators/core/api/v1alpha1/clientinstance_types.go):
Field Meaning app the application identity. Drives the core.runink.org/app label and the dedicated-taint toleration. tenant the tenant key. The core.runink.org/tenant label plus soft node affinity. role controlplane or runner (default runner): selects the PriorityClass. image the container image to run. port the container and service port (default 8080). replicas default 1; ignored when suspend is true. computeUnits a sizing budget, mapped to real CPU and memory limits. It is not the billed Compute Unit (one model-slot second); see Plans and billing. tags client labels added to the pod template and ServiceAccount. placement nodeSelector, tolerations (added to the defaults), affinity (replaces the default soft affinity). env extra environment variables. users access grants: email, role (admin, writer or reader, default reader), optional phone, optional expiresAt. Projected as AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS and AUTH_SEED_USERS. subscription tier (lite, dedicated or enterprise), seats, status (active, suspended or past_due). suspend scale the instance down. DeepCopy is written by hand (there is no controller-gen), and the CRD YAML is the authority. The CRD schema prunes unknown fields, so a field that is not in the schema is silently dropped (this is how a subscription.credits field was lost on every write before it was removed). The old spec.variant field was removed in core#903, because the env vars it projected had no reader.
Every operator gives each pod the same isolation labels and scheduling (operators/placement): core.runink.org/{app,tenant,role}, runink.org/{app,tenant,role}, the toleration core.runink.org/dedicated=, soft (anti-)affinity and a priorityClassName. Namespace-level policy (ResourceQuota, LimitRange, PriorityClass, NetworkPolicy, PDB) is static kustomize under grpc/infrastructure/apps/*/kustomize/governance/.
data.images#Images:
core build builds local podman images only. The images the cluster runs come from .github/workflows/core-images-build.yml: werf and buildah in a privileged, ephemeral in-cluster Job, pushed to the node-local registry. Every Dockerfile takes its base image through ARG BASE_REGISTRY and pins an @sha256: digest. The base images are declared in grpc/infrastructure/images/baseimages.yaml and mirrored with core images mirror.
After a CD roll (core-cd.yml), workloads run a digest-pinned :latest@sha256:…. A bare kubectl rollout restart then restarts onto the same digest. To move a workload onto new bits, dispatch core-cd.yml with images=.
data.inference#Inference: The model plane is sovereign: no hosted model is called. mistral.rs is the only engine. The llama.cpp image was retired on 2026-09-27. cmd/modelrouter is the one admission queue in front of the engines. Budgets across the agents derive from one configured decode rate, INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S. See Models and inference.
data.networking#Networking: The decided pod network is dual-stack, IPv6 primary (owner decision 2026-09-26). Until the River/distro k0s change ships, the running box is still IPv6 single-stack, and the local multipass clusters are k0s’s default IPv4 single-stack. Manifests must therefore work on all three. The IPv4 ranges are written in one place (grpc/infrastructure/apps/_shared/cluster-cidrs/), and dual_stack_manifests_test.go enforces the rules: bind [::], build URLs with net.JoinHostPort, never pin a Service to one family, and give every IPv6 egress catch-all its IPv4 twin.
data.the-code-by-module#The code, by module:
Module Where Contents github.com/org-runink/core grpc/ the core CLI (grpc/cmd/core), the other grpc/cmd/* binaries, grpc/infrastructure/*, the agent fleet under grpc/agents/ github.com/org-runink/face-operator grpc/operators/runink the FACE Kubernetes operator github.com/org-runink/pulse-operator grpc/operators/pulse the PULSE Kubernetes operator github.com/org-runink/core-operator grpc/operators/core the generic ClientInstance CRD and its controller, the provisioner, and the TIDE console github.com/org-runink/placement grpc/operators/placement shared pod placement and envcontract, the declared set of required env vars per app and role The operators are separate modules on purpose, to keep controller-runtime’s dependency tree out of the root module. go build ./... at the root does not cover them.
The shared libraries are separate repositories (inference, security, mesh, store, ml, and ui for the shared Flutter and gRPC components). TIDE consumes them through local replace directives. For image builds it also carries committed copies of some of them (grpc/vendor/ and .github/*-snapshot/), which one guard test, grpc/operators/runink/internal/controller/sibling_copies_test.go, keeps in step with their upstream.
data.traffic-the-edge-and-the-apps#Traffic: t:
Each app’s web UI is served by its own small Go frontend (the “sleeve”, in the app repo), which serves the Flutter bundle and reverse-proxies gRPC-web, /auth/* and /api/* to the backend. The devgateway edge routes / on each host to that frontend.
The devgateway has its own sign-in gate. When edge auth is on, an empty DEVGW_AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS now refuses every sign-in. Admitting any verified Google account needs the explicit DEVGW_AUTH_ALLOW_ANY_VERIFIED=true. Edge sessions are server-side, in the devgateway’s own appfs root.
FORGE has no domain and no sign-in of its own. TIDE serves it at /forge/ through its own reverse proxy, under TIDE’s session, and vouches for the person with the X-Core-Identity header.
data.trust-the-security-spine#Trust: the secu:
Everything internal is zero-trust:
PKI. security/pki is an in-memory ECDSA CA that issues short-lived leaves off a shared cluster CA. Verification is chain-only, so peers dial by service DNS or pod IP. core mesh ca mints and distributes that CA. Encryption at rest. security/secrets/envelope is AES-GCM envelope encryption, applied unconditionally by store/objectstore and store/connections. There is no switch to turn it off. Anything that opens either store needs CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK and refuses to start without it. The object store. TIDE runs its own S3-compatible objectd (from the store library), not the MinIO server. objectd verifies SigV4, and core-operator’s provisioner mints every objectd key as an objectd-key- Secret in the consumer’s namespace. App databases. FACE and PULSE seal database values per column before they are written. That is a narrower claim than “the database is encrypted”: schema, table and column names, row counts and unsealed columns stay readable. Whole-database encryption is an open decision. Committed key material: none. core dev up generates its local KEK with crypto/rand on first run, and a test flags any 32-byte key literal in that package.
data.what-runs-on-the-cluster#What runs on th:
Deployments use k0s with pure kustomize overlays (no Helm). The operators are the authoritative source of each pod’s spec and env, not the kustomize base YAML: to change what a pod gets, change the controller in operators/{runink,pulse,core}/internal/controller/.
The console tracks these namespaces: core-system (TIDE), runink-system (FACE), pulse-system (PULSE), luna-system (LUNA), forge-system (FORGE), inference-system, github-runners (CI) and registry-system.
data.what-tide-is-and-what-it-is-not#What TID:
TIDE is the shared platform for the Runink applications (FACE, PULSE, LUNA and FORGE). Platform concerns live here: self-healing, the event mesh, secrets, the object store, inference serving, MCP, PKI and mTLS, telemetry, the Kubernetes operators and the infrastructure as code.
The apps do not import TIDE. Code that more than one app runs lives in a shared library that TIDE and the apps both import. FACE, PULSE, LUNA and FORGE each carry a test that fails if their go.mod or any import names github.com/org-runink/core.
data.where-the-console-keeps-its-data#Where t:
The console does not keep its metadata in ConfigMaps. It mounts its own encrypted store/appfs root for the app core-console (appfsroot.go, metastore.go, metadoc.go):
on objectd, when OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT and both credentials are set. If objectd is configured but cannot be opened, the console fails closed instead of falling back; otherwise on a local encrypted fallback under CONSOLE_APPFS_DIR (default /var/lib/core/appfs), on its PVC. There is no in-memory mode. Each store (agent health, schedules, runs, lineage, governance findings, judgements, rules reconciliation, session commands and runs, GitHub config, cloud providers, connections, subscriptions) is a table in that root. Sessions are run/sessions. The audit chain is var/log/audit: a hash chain that continues across restarts and that GET /api/audit/verify walks.
Only three ConfigMaps are still written, because agent workflows read them: core-agent-schedules, core-judgement-submissions and core-console-connections. The console republishes them from its tables after every commit, so editing one by hand changes nothing: the next write replaces it.

data:
Runink TIDE is sold on its own, separately from FACE and PULSE. FORGE is part of TIDE: a TIDE plan includes it. Every product has the same three plan categories, and the category says where the work runs, which decides how compute is charged.
The price list is served by the console at GET /api/plans?product=core, which needs no sign-in.
data.compute-units#Compute Units:
1 CU is one second of a model slot, so 3,600 CU is one slot-hour. A slot is one request’s hold on the shared model plane. CU is charged only on Lite, where the work runs on Runink’s hardware. Dedicated and Enterprise are unmetered: their compute runs on your own infrastructure.
On Lite Rule Allowance 18,000 CU a seat a month (5 slot-hours), pooled across the subscription’s seats Over the allowance pay as you go at $0.10 per 100 CU, billed per started block of 100 CU Prepaid CU bought in advance for a month at 10% off, or for a year at 20% off. Unused prepaid CU lapses at the end of its period. Prepaid CU extends a Lite allowance only Fair use at most 900 CU a seat in any rolling hour (15 slot-minutes). Work past that queues: it is never refused and never billed extra
data.cu-is-not-speccomputeunits#CU is not \u0: ClientInstance.spec.computeUnits is a sizing budget for an instance’s pod, not the billed unit. The operator maps it to CPU and memory limits (2 millicores and 8 MiB per unit, between 0.5 and 8 CPU and between 1 and 32 GiB). The FinOps view on Intelligence › Dashboards (CFO Cockpit) multiplies that allocation by the $0.10 per 100 CU rate and labels the result cu-estimate with measure: allocation: it is showback of what was allocated, an estimate, never a charge, and never the metered usage the Billing page shows.
data.currency-and-billing-periods#Currency an: One list, in US dollars. /api/plans and the /api/checkout quote are in US cents. Your regional currency. Billing converts the list into the currency of the purchaser’s country with the European Central Bank’s euro reference rates. The rate is the one in force when the month opens: the last ECB publication before the 1st, fixed for the whole month. Seat prices round to a whole unit of the local currency; usage lines and fees round to its minor unit (cents). A country without a mapped currency is billed in US dollars. A missing or stale rate stops the bill. It is never billed as 0 and never at another rate. Anniversary periods. A period runs from the day of the month your subscription started, 00:00 UTC, to the same day the next month. A start on the 31st bills to the last day of a shorter month (February 28, or 29 in a leap year), then returns to the 31st.
data.how-cu-is-measured#How CU is measured:
The model router (cmd/modelrouter, see Models and inference) is the one place that sees both when a request was admitted to a slot and when its response finished. On every response it reports:
X-Runink-Queue-Ms, a header: how long the request waited for a slot; X-Runink-Slot-Ms, an HTTP trailer: how long the request held the slot, from admission to the end of the proxied body, net of any time the engine spent waking from zero. Queue wait is never billed. The caller attributes the slot time to the billing account from its own verified session. Billing sums the milliseconds for the period and converts to CU once, rounding up, so a period with any usage at all bills at least 1 CU.
Controls on that path:
The router never charges anyone. It measures; it does not know who pays. Metering never blocks a request. When the trailer cannot reach the caller (for example, the client disconnected mid-stream), the request still completes, and the gap is logged (modelrouter: metering gap reason=…) and counted in /status as metering_gaps. A missing trailer records nothing: never a guessed figure. One rule for every product. FACE and TIDE record and read compute units with the same shared recorder and meter, so a slot-second costs the same CU in both. Who pays for the console’s own model calls (Ask TIDE, the grounded Ask, the console chat, and voice transcription). By default, the signed-in person’s purchaser: their own subscription, or the subscription their seat is on. This is the same account the Billing page shows, so every person’s usage lands on the allowance they see. CORE_BILLING_ACCOUNT is left unset by default. Set it only on a single-purchaser installation where every call should bill one account whoever asked; when set, it overrides the per-session purchaser. Unattributed usage. A call with no signed-in person, or from a person with no subscription and no seat, is recorded against the platform account and counted as unattributed. It stays visible in the ledger and the console’s metering counters, and it is never invoiced to anyone. Unmeasured sites are listed below, each with the reason. An unmeasured site records nothing; it is never estimated. Each product is metered separately. A TIDE subscription’s Billing page counts only TIDE’s ledgers (the console and FORGE). A purchaser’s FACE or PULSE usage counts against that product’s own allowance and is never pooled into TIDE’s. The Billing page shows given against used for the current anniversary period: the plan’s CU allowance, the CU measured so far, and the period’s start and end. With no current period on record, the page says compute units are not measured rather than showing a lifetime total. An app instance TIDE runs for a subscriber (FACE, PULSE) receives the same period as SUBSCRIPTION_PERIOD_END (and SUBSCRIPTION_ANNUAL), so its own Billing page shows the same window; an instance with no period on record shows usage as unmeasured. Platform work is never billed. TIDE’s own agents on their own triggers (the reviewer, fixer, curator and the rest, on a schedule, a pull request or a mention) carry no billing account and are never metered. Agents a person dispatches are billed to that person’s purchaser. A Trust › Harness dispatch, or an Atlas playbook run a person started, carries an opaque, expiring billing grant in the GitHub dispatch; the purchaser itself stays in the console and never reaches GitHub. The agent run sends a console-signed billing claim to the model router on each call, reads the router’s slot trailer, and reports it with an event id it reuses on retry, so a retried report is never counted twice. A grant accepts at most 2,000 reports and can never record more slot time than the wall time since it was issued. A run nobody attributable started (a schedule, an event-triggered playbook, a person with no TIDE subscription or seat) gets no grant: it is unmeasured and counted, never billed to the platform account or anyone else.
data.seats-subscriptions-and-the-billing-page: Seats are managed on the instance’s Admin page, through the billing seat routes (/api/billing/seats). Nobody changes their own access, the last admin stays, and a full seat pool refuses an invite. See Trust and access. One subscription per email. Every route that starts a checkout (/api/signup, /api/checkout and the Billing page) refuses a second subscription for the same purchaser. The public signup is gated by reCAPTCHA when it is configured. Checkout goes through Stripe, and only when the installation configures it (STRIPE_SECRET_KEY). Without it the quote still works and the page says billing is not configured. A Dedicated plan can name its cloud account at checkout (cloudTenant: a GCP project, a Databricks workspace or a Snowflake account). A Lite plan naming one is refused, because Lite runs on shared hardware and has no runners of its own. Entitlement fails closed. A subscription is entitled only while it is active, trialing or past due; anything else, an unknown plan, or an unreadable subscription record grants no plan, never Lite and never a free tier. The Billing page (opened from Account) is the shared org-runink/ui billing component. It shows a usage figure only where a meter feeds it: an unmeasured value is shown as unmeasured, never as zero, and an estimate is never shown as a charge. For where TIDE can deploy a runner, and what a connected runner does, see Runners.
data.the-three-categories#The three categorie:
TIDE Lite TIDE Dedicated TIDE Enterprise Where the work runs Runink’s shared hardware, spot-style runners in your own cloud account: GCP, Databricks or Snowflake your premises (on-prem runners) or your own cloud account Priced per seat (a person), 1–9 seats node (a machine), from 1 node custom quote Price $75 a seat a month billed yearly, or $89 a seat month to month $249 a month for the first node, then $149 a month for each extra node; yearly contract custom Compute 18,000 CU a seat a month, metered unlimited CU, on your own cloud bill unlimited CU Other charges CU over the allowance (below) 1% of the runners’ cloud cost none on on-prem runners There is no node fee and no flat platform fee on any plan: the plan’s platformMonthlyCents is 0. On-prem runners are Enterprise only. A yearly price is charged as twelve times the monthly rate.
The seat or node count must fit the plan’s band, or the quote is refused with the band’s minSeats and maxSeats. A Dedicated plan offered month to month is refused with “this plan is annual-only; retry with annual=true”. Enterprise returns no quote: /api/checkout answers custom: true and directs you to sales.
data.where-compute-units-are-measured#Where c: Site State How Ask TIDE, the grounded Ask, console chat Measured through the model router; the slot trailer, against the signed-in person’s purchaser Voice transcription Measured through the model router’s voice (voxtral) tier, the same rule as chat. Only a console with no router configured dials the voice engine directly, and each such call is a counted gap Agents a person dispatches (Harness, playbooks) Measured the dispatch’s billing grant: the slot trailer of each call, against the dispatching person’s purchaser Text-to-speech Not measured the speech service (ttsd) is not behind the model router, which has no speech-synthesis tier, and it reports no slot time of its own. A self-reported figure would be a second meter outside the router’s queue, so nothing is recorded FORGE verify runs Not measured runner time on GitHub Actions; the verify dispatch carries no purchaser account Agents on their own triggers (cron, PR events, mentions) Not measured the platform’s own work: never billed

This page lists every row on the console rail, in rail order, with its link name and what it reads.
The structure is defined in one place, flutter/lib/core/widgets/nav.dart. It is pinned by flutter/test/nav_ia_test.dart. The labels come from flutter/lib/l10n/app_en.arb. Link to any page with ?tab=, for example https:///?tab=runners. Names are case-insensitive. An unknown name opens Overview.
On 2026-09-28 the rail was reduced twice, both times with the owner’s approval:
The consolidation took it from 44 rows to 29. The nav cut took it from 29 rows to 16, and moved Admin to the footer. Each time, a page that was a second view of one subject became a sub-tab, persona or panel of the page that owns that subject. Every old ?tab= name still works and opens the exact view. See Link names that still work.

data.footer#Footer:
The instance row names the instance the console acts for, and your role on it. Choosing it reopens the instance cards.
Admin (admin) sits directly under the instance row, and only if you are an admin of that instance. It manages that instance’s members and seats, through the shared access service.
Account is the shared profile page. It shows:
your sign-in method and session expiry; the instances you hold a live grant on; Runink TIDE’s GitHub configuration, cloud providers and legal sections. Billing is its own page, opened from Account.
A subscriber sees only their home, the instance row, Admin (if they administer the instance) and Account.
